The court does not have the
items.body: The exterior of the Idaho Supreme Court building in Boise as seen on Jan. 14, 2026. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) The Idaho Supreme Court on Friday unanimously ruled that state officials must redraft explanations of the effect of voting for or against the proposed abortion rights initiative that will appear on voters’ Nov. 3 general election ballots. The court does not have the authority to write new language, but told the offices of the Idaho Attorney General and Secretary of State that they must submit revised ballot language to the court by 5 p.m. Saturday — around 24 hours after the decision was entered. Idaho Supreme Court Justice Gregory Moeller, right, asks a question during a hearing in this April 25, 2025, file photo. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) The decision, written by Justice Gregory Moeller, found that neither the “yes” or “no” effect statements met the law’s requirements. “A statement is not ‘clear’ if it leaves voters uncertain about a principal legal consequence of their choice, and it does not describe ‘the effect’ of a vote if it materially misstates that consequence,” Moeller wrote. “Conciseness permits Respondents to omit unnecessary detail; it does not permit them to convey an inaccurate picture of the effect of a specific vote.” The ballot “effect statements,” required under state law to be a clear and concise explanation of the impacts of a yes or no vote, were written by Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador and Secretary of State Phil McGrane. The state’s high court heard oral arguments Wednesday and issued a speedy ruling as election officials neared a Sept. 11 deadline to be able to send ballots to military and overseas voters. Supporters of the initiative, called Prop 1, filed a lawsuit on Aug. 27, arguing that the drafted effect statements of “yes” or “no” votes on the ballot measure were “misleading” and “confusing.” Attorneys representing Labrador and McGrane defended the statements in court, arguing they were the clearest and shortest way to inform voters. Joe Parris, a spokesperson for the secretary of state, said Friday the office is working to comply with the order. “We appreciate the Idaho Supreme Court’s prompt review of Proposition One yes-and-no effect statements,” Parris said in an email. “As directed by the court, we are working closely with the Attorney General’s Office to prepare and submit revised statements. We remain focused on meeting all necessary deadlines to ensure ballots are printed and distributed on schedule.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. The proposed initiative, drafted by the group Idahoans United for Women and Families, would repeal Idaho’s strict abortion ban, allowing abortions up to fetal viability or beyond in cases of a medical emergency. It would also enumerate rights related to reproductive healthcare, such as access to contraception and IVF, and privacy in healthcare decisions. Under Idaho’s abortion laws, it is a felony to perform nearly any abortion, except to prevent the death of the mother, or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors may also be sued for a minimum of $20,000 for performing an abortion. items.summary: Idaho’s abortion ban applies to any stage of pregnancy, with affirmative defenses for cases of rape and incest with an accompanying police report and if an abortion is necessary to save a patient’s life. (Photo illustration by Getty Images) A panel of judges has placed on hold a federal court order protecting an Idaho fetal medicine doctor from prosecution for abortions performed in specific circu
items.body: Idaho’s abortion ban applies to any stage of pregnancy, with affirmative defenses for cases of rape and incest with an accompanying police report and if an abortion is necessary to save a patient’s life. (Photo illustration by Getty Images) A panel of judges has placed on hold a federal court order protecting an Idaho fetal medicine doctor from prosecution for abortions performed in specific circumstances. The order means Idaho’s abortion laws are fully in effect, with only exemptions to protect the life of the mother, or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester if a police report has been filed. Doctors who perform abortions outside of those exemptions face felony penalties and revocation or suspension of their medical license. Idaho federal judge narrows abortion ruling to only protect Boise doctor who filed lawsuit The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals panel on Thursday blocked a ruling that would’ve carved out new exemptions in Idaho’s strict abortion ban for the doctor challenging the law. The order will be in place until Ninth Circuit judges are scheduled to hear arguments on Sept. 22. Previously, U.S. District of Idaho Court Judge B. Lynn Winmill wrote in an 81-page decision on Aug. 13 that abortions could be performed in cases where the mother faced serious health risks or risk of self-harm, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. However, after Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador appealed the ruling, Winmill n arrowed the decision to only protect the doctor who filed the lawsuit challenging Idaho’s abortion ban, Dr. Stacy Seyb. Seyb, represented by attorneys from the Lawyering Project and Legal Voice, challenged the constitutionality of Idaho abortion ban’s limited exceptions “The Constitution protects pregnant people’s access to life- and health-preserving abortion care,” Lawyering Project Executive Director Stephanie Toti said in an email to the Sun “We are hopeful that the court of appeals will allow that care to resume after it hears oral argument later this month.” Idaho Family Policy Center attorneys file brief in support of law on half of Idaho lawmakers Attorneys with the Idaho Family Policy Center, a conservative Christian lobbying group, filed a brief in support of Idaho’s abortion ban on behalf of 54 Idaho state legislators. Idaho Family Policy Center Legal Director Caleb Pirc wrote that Winmill’s decision went beyond his authority. “The district court improperly made policy for the people of Idaho,” Pirc wrote. “It may have thought its policy was better than the Legislature’s, but that was not its judgment to make.” The brief says that the authority to create abortion policy rests solely with the Legislature. The lawmakers represented by the brief include 37 House representatives and 17 senators, all Republicans, including leaders from both chambers. (Photo courtesy of Todd Wernex/Idaho Department of Lands) State officials announced the temporary closure of seven trails on Thursday due to the Crooked Fire that is burning near Idaho City. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE The fire is burning in steep, rocky and heavily forested terrain about 14 miles northeast of Idaho City, along the North Fork of the Boise River. Idaho Department of Lands officials said the temporary closures are necessary to protect the public and firefighters’ safety as the wildfire continues to burn. The temporary trail closures include: 694, Granite Creek 692, Peg’s Leg 664, Kevin’s Hand 660, North Fork of Thorn 594, Bannock Loop 123, Easter Creek 110, Chuck Wells The closures apply to everyone, including all motorized and nonmotorized recreation users, officials said. “ Please do not enter closed areas or bypass posted closure signs,” Idaho Department of Lands officials wrote in a press release. “Giving firefighters the room they need is critical to yours and their safety and allows them to focus on protecting our communities, property and public lands. ” Need to get in touch? Have a news tip? CONTACT US The seven new temporary trail closures are in addition to existing closures the U.S. Forest Service announced Aug. 23 , which are scheduled to remain in place until Dec. 31 unless rescinded earlier. Those closures affect the Black Rock Campground, Upper Crooked River Trailhead and Lower Crooked River Trailhead, officials said. The Crooked Fire is a human-caused fire that started Aug. 18 outside of Idaho City. The cause of the fire, which has burned 9,956 acres, is under investigation, officials said. Crews are using a full-suppression strategy where conditions allow them to do so safely, officials said. There were about 600 personnel fighting the Crooked Fire as of Thursday, as well as eight helicopters, 22 engines and 14 pieces of heavy equipment, according to Great Basin Incident Management Team 3. Containment was estimated at 21% as of Thursday. Updated information on the Crooked Fire is posted online by the U.S. Forest Service-Boise National Forest and the U.S. government’s interagency Incident Information System InciWeb. items.body: Educators, lawmakers, students and architects gathered in Boise and Star Wednesday to celebrate the groundbreakings of two new schools. The projects will give hundreds of students in the West Ada and Middleton districts new classrooms in 2027 and 2028 — and get some of those students out of portables. The projects have something in common: Neither district passed a local bond measure or increased property taxes to fund them. “The most important thing is that we’re getting this school built,” House Speaker Mike Moyle, R-Star, told EdNews at the Middleton groundbreaking in Star. “The second most important thing is that we’re getting it done without raising property taxes.” Students at a groundbreaking for the rebuilt Lake Hazel Elementary in the West Ada School District on Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026. After the national anthem, Middleton Superintendent Marc Gee had attendees recite the Pledge of Allegiance — fitting for a school named Freedom with an Eagle mascot. Freedom will alleviate overcrowding in the district’s three elementary schools, which have reached as much as 150% capacity. Wednesday’s attendees included Moyle, state superintendent Debbie Critchfield, Sen. Tammy Nichols of Middleton and Rep. Bruce Skaug of Nampa. Also there were Middleton Mayor Tim O’Meara and Star Mayor Trevor Chadwick, who addressed the crowd to tout the process for funding the schools. “N o property tax dollars are paying for this. No property tax dollars paid for the other one,” Chadwick said, referring to West Ada’s recently completed Independence Elementary , also in Star. “ That’s the way it should be.” The $19.1 million Freedom Elementary, a project in Middleton’s sights since around 2015, will serve 400 students, with the ability to extend a wing of the school to bring future capacity to 700. Funding did not come from a locally approved bond, the way school construction projects are typically bankrolled in Idaho. Local voters rejected five consecutive bond measures, helping Middleton to qualify for $11.1 million from previously untapped state money: the Public School Facilities Cooperative Fund . items.title: Idaho U.S. Senate candidate David Roth removes name from general election ballot
items.summary: This article was first published in the Idaho Capital Sun Idaho Democrat David Roth, who had been running for the U.S. Senate seat held by Idaho Republican Jim Risch, officially withdrew his name from the ballot just days before the deadline. Roth submitted his withdrawal form on Aug. 28, citing a “lack of support from Democratic Party,” according to the form obtained by the Idaho Capital Sun in a
items.body: This article was first published in the Idaho Capital Sun Idaho Democrat David Roth, who had been running for the U.S. Senate seat held by Idaho Republican Jim Risch, officially withdrew his name from the ballot just days before the deadline. Roth submitted his withdrawal form on Aug. 28, citing a “lack of support from Democratic Party,” according to the form obtained by the Idaho Capital Sun in a public records request. A spokesperson for the Idaho Democratic Party declined to comment. Roth faced pressure from fellow Democrats to clear way for independent candidate Roth announced he was ending his campaign on July 28, the Idaho Capital Sun reported. He had faced strong pressure from supporters of independent candidate Todd Achilles, who argued an independent had a better chance of defeating the longtime incumbent in a head-to-head race. Roth did not endorse Achilles. Roth told the Sun he didn’t want to drop out, but he felt like he didn’t have a choice. He’d also received a letter from leaders of Ada County Democrats asking him to drop out , the Spokesman-Review reported. “Without support from Ada County, I mean that really hindered fundraising or campaign ability,” Roth told the Sun in a phone interview. “And when you have so many people who hold leadership positions in the party advocating for a candidate besides their nominee, it makes it really just impossible.” Roth’s most recent federal election filing shows he garnered about $14,600 in contributions but that his campaign had about $10,100 in debts and loans to be paid back, as of June 30. Roth ran for federal office in 2022 and 2024 and for the state Legislature in 2020. He said this run was “probably the worst experience I’ve ever been through in my entire life.” “And I’ve been through a lot,” he said. (Photo by Mia Maldonado/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s state prison system has entered into a formal agreement with federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE. It’s the second state agency to join the federal immigration program. The Idaho Department of Correction on Aug. 28 joined the 287(g ) program, which allows local law enforcement to carry out some limited immigration enforcement with supervision from federal authorities, according to ICE records of participating agencies. Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little gives his State of the State Address from the House chambers on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “Idaho has a responsibility to uphold the rule of law and protect the people of our state,” Gov. Brad Little said in a press release. “This agreement gives Idaho another tool to make sure criminal aliens who are subject to federal immigration enforcement are transferred to federal custody when they have completed their Idaho sentences. Idaho will continue working with the Trump administration to secure our communities and support the enforcement of our nation’s laws.” The state prison agency’s agreement follows what’s called the “warrant service” model, which allows designated officers within the agency to serve warrants to undocumented people in custody. The agreement “formalizes a process IDOC has already been using to assist ICE,” according to a press release from the governor’s office. Correction staff have historically provided ICE with information on inmates with felony convictions to allow the federal agents to identify those who may be subject to immigration detainers, which are requests by ICE to hold individuals to prevent the release of people who may be undocumented, the release said. Bree Derrick (Photo from Idaho Department of Correction) “IDOC has a longstanding responsibility to coordinate with our federal partners when individuals in our custody are subject to federal immigration enforcement,” IDOC Director Bree Derrick said in the press release. “This agreement strengthens that coordination and gives our department a clear, formal process for serving ICE warrants and transferring individuals into federal custody when their Idaho sentences are complete.” The state prison agency also “facilitates due process hearings for individuals undergoing deportation proceedings and coordinates with ICE when Idaho sentences are satisfied,” the release said. In June 2025 , Idaho State Police entered a 287(g) agreement with ICE to help transport state inmates to federal detention facilities for deportation. This agreement was funded by the governor’s office emergency funds. As of May, ISP had transported more than 80 people out of correctional facilities, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. An Idaho Capital Sun analysis found some cases where charges were dismissed or still pending when the person was transported to an ICE facility. ISP leaders later said the agency changed its procedure to ensure convictions were secured before transporting individuals. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. EdNews filed the complaint last month after trustees voted on “Item E” following a July 29 executive session, a closed portion of a public meeting. The item was not listed as an action item, and no details were posted. Idaho Code 74-204(4) requires an agenda to identify an item as an “action item” when it requires a vote, providing notice to the public that action may be taken. EdNews discovered through a public records request that the item was a settlement between the district and Old Republic Surety Company, which held the bond for a company that did faulty work on a sidewalk replacement project. items.body: Voters on Tuesday elected Andy Hawes to serve a four-year term on the Boise school board. Hawes received 2,430 votes, or 50.93%, to candidate Kirt Naylor’s 2,341 votes, or 49.07%. Just 3.9% of registered voters participated in Tuesday’s election. This will be Hawes’ second time serving as a trustee for Boise Independent School District. Trustees in 2011 appointed Hawes to fill a vacancy and voters in 2022 elected him to a four-year term. He resigned one year into that term, however, to take a job in Seattle as senior corporate counsel for timber company Weyerhaeuser. He moved back to Boise in March to work as director of land, water and asset recovery for J.R. Simplot Company. He told EdNews in July that he plans on staying in Boise. “This is my dream job and I’m here for the long haul,” he said. “I’m invested in the community.” Andy Hawes and Kirt Naylor (Campaign photos) " data-large-file="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Hawes-and-Naylor-1180x784.jpg" class="wp-image-122217 size-full" src="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Hawes-and-Naylor.jpg" alt="" width="1920" height="1275" srcset="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Hawes-and-Naylor.jpg 1920w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Hawes-and-Naylor-620x412.jpg 620w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Hawes-and-Naylor-1180x784.jpg 1180w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Hawes-and-Naylor-200x133.jpg 200w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Hawes-and-Naylor-1536x1020.jpg 1536w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1920px) 100vw, 1920px" /> Andy Hawes and Kirt Naylor (Campaign photos) In a candidate forum last week at Boise High, Hawes said the biggest issue facing the district is declining enrollment. He said the district needs to see facilities as assets. If the district considers closing a school, he would try to find creative ways to use the building to support the community. “Are there other uses that we can use for facilities that would fit squarely with what the community wants in serving students?” Hawes said. During his time on the school board, Hawes helped create the Board of Trustees Student Advisory Committee. High school students meet with the board and administrators to provide feedback and input on decisions. He has also served on the board of directors for Jesse Tree of Idaho, a nonprofit that prevents homelessness and eviction This is the second time Naylor has come in second place for a seat on the board. He applied and interviewed for a vacancy in October. Trustees selected Alejandro Necochea to fill the vacancy, and Naylor was the runner up. While most elections in Idaho take place in May and November, Boise Independent School District has its own charter that allows it to conduct elections on the first Tuesday in September every other year. All seats are at-large, meaning there are no zones within the district. Hawes will be sworn into office during the district’s regular board meeting on Sept. 14.

(Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) Months after protestors wouldn’t leave the lobby of the Idaho governor’s office in an attempt to meet with him over anti-transgender bills, a jury on Tuesday found a local minister guilty on a misdemeanor trespassing charge. The jury found the Rev. Sara LaWall — who wore a clerical collar under a rainbow speckled blazer as she sat in court — guilty of trespassing after prosecutors said she remained in the governor’s office after being warned it was closed for the night during a protest of anti-trans bills this spring. Idaho’s transgender bathroom ban is now the law. How will police enforce it? That’s still unclear. After the jury delivered the verdict, LaWall, the minister for the Boise Unitarian Universalist Fellowship, told reporters that the possible prison sentence she could face would be less time than judges can dole out for violations of Idaho’s new criminal transgender bathroom ban . “That just feels wholly unfair and outsized and ridiculous,” LaWall told reporters after her trial. “… The jury found me guilty of staying in the governor’s office after being told to leave. I didn’t dispute those facts. But someone going to the bathroom now has a higher sentence, and that just feels so disproportionate and so wrong.” Under state law , her trespassing charge is punishable by up to six months in prison. The state’s bathroom ban allows for up to a year in prison on a first offense and up to five years on repeat offenses. Minutes after the nearly full-day trial finished Tuesday, the jury reached its verdict. LaWall will be sentenced on the charge later. Idaho 4th District Judge Adam Kimball scheduled her sentencing for Sept. 17. LaWall’s attorney requested her sentencing be delayed instead of issued Tuesday evening. She hopes at her sentencing she can share more about why she was at the governor’s office. “I have really mixed feelings,” LaWall said of the verdict. “It’s hard not to feel a little emotional about the verdict, but I don’t — I’m not entirely surprised. I took the stand and said as much as the judge allowed me to say about why we were there, which wasn’t very much, and that was disappointing to me to not be able to tell more of the story about why we were there.” LaWall was one of nine protestors who were arrested on trespassing charges at the April 1 protest. At the protest, LaWall and others waited in the lobby in the governor’s office for more than three hours. The protest came a day after Gov. items.body: Three Idaho charter schools provide vastly different paths to getting students down the graduation line. Students at Valor Classical Academy follow a set of six virtues, including self-government and perseverance. A student wants to be a mom when she grows up. Students at Idaho Arts Charter School can take dance, choir, piano, ceramics and theatre. General education classes often have an art aspect. One student wants to be a silversmith, another wants to teach guitar. Students at Elevate Academy Nampa take classes in eight trades, including construction, medical arts and culinary. One student wants to graduate as a certified nursing assistant and join the military. The Idaho Charter School Association last week hosted tours of public charter schools in Caldwell, Middleton, Nampa and Kuna for legislators and journalists. “They’re making big decisions for our schools and we want to make sure that they have all the knowledge and information they need about charters to make really informed decisions,” Executive Director Nanette Merrill said. The organization invited all legislators and candidates from districts 10 and 22, but only Sen. Tammy Nichols, R-Middleton, and candidates Nancy Parker and Loren Petty showed up. On Thursday, attendees visited Valor Classical Academy in Kuna, Idaho Arts Charter School in Nampa and Elevate Academy Nampa. Each tour included pre-planned classroom visits followed by a panel discussion with selected parents and students. items.body: Every two years, something unusual happens in Idaho: every single member of the Legislature is up for election. All 70 members of the Idaho House face the voters. So do all 35 members of the Idaho Senate. That means every legislator in Boise operates on essentially the same political clock. Every two years, every seat is on the ballot, every incumbent is potentially campaigning, and every member knows the next primary is never far away. We should change that. Idaho should keep two-year terms for members of the House but move state senators to four-year terms, staggered so roughly half the Senate is elected every two years. It would make the Senate more deliberative, provide greater continuity in state government, reduce some of the election-year incentives for political theater and strengthen the Legislature’s ability to serve as a check on the permanent bureaucracy. Most importantly, it would create a meaningful institutional difference between Idaho’s two legislative chambers. After all, if we’re going to have a House and a Senate, they shouldn’t simply be two versions of the same thing. The Idaho Constitution currently gives representatives and senators the same two-year terms. The House is larger and the Senate smaller, but members of both chambers face voters on precisely the same schedule. That’s not how most states do it. And there is a reason. The two chambers of a legislature are supposed to serve somewhat different purposes. The House should be the chamber closest to the people and most immediately responsive to shifts in public opinion. Its members should return to voters frequently. Two-year terms make sense. The Senate should be different. A Senate is traditionally the smaller and more deliberative legislative body. Its members should have greater opportunity to take a longer view, develop expertise and provide continuity as political winds change. That doesn’t make senators more important than representatives. It gives them a different institutional role. Consider the political life of a newly elected Idaho senator. Win an election in November. Go to Boise in January. Serve one legislative session. Spend the interim knowing another election is approaching. Return for a second session—and by then the primary election is only months away. Then start all over again. There is barely time to govern before it’s time to campaign. Today, every one of Idaho’s 105 legislative seats appears on the ballot at the same time. Theoretically, a single election could send 105 brand-new legislators to Boise. Some Idahoans might hear that and say: Good. There is something appealing about a clean sweep. Turnover can bring fresh ideas, disrupt comfortable relationships and remind elected officials that the offices they occupy belong to the people. But there is another side to that equation. If every legislator is new, state government isn’t. The agencies are still there. The departments are still there. The administrative rules, budget processes and government programs are still there. And the career employees who have spent years—or decades—working inside that system are still there. One of the Legislature’s most important responsibilities is overseeing the executive branch and the permanent bureaucracy beneath it. Lawmakers control appropriations, write the laws agencies implement and are supposed to ask hard questions on behalf of taxpayers. To do that effectively, legislators need expertise of their own. That’s an important point for those of us who believe in limited government. Limiting government isn’t only about asking how much power government possesses. We should also care about where that power resides and who exercises it. items.body: A Flock Automated License Plate Reader near the Lowe's on Overland Road in Boise, as captured on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Valentin Termite/Idaho Capital Sun) Congressman Russ Fulcher, R-Idaho (Photo courtesy of Russ Fulcher’s official website) Idaho Republican U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher signed on to federal legislation to limit federal law enforcement’s access to data from automated license plate readers, like Flock cameras, and other surveillance equipment. Fulcher announced Monday in a press release that he is co-sponsoring H.R. 9716 , called the Protecting Rights in Video and Equipment Acquired Discovery Act, or Privacy Act. The legislation would, in most cases, require federal law enforcement to obtain a warrant from a federal judge before accessing surveillance data from state and local systems, including cameras that capture images of vehicle occupants, long-range microphones, electronic fingerprint detection technology, and “substantially similar technology” as determined by the U.S. attorney general, according to the press release. “I’m proud to sign on to this legislation to protect the privacy rights of Idahoans from increasingly intrusive surveillance data collection and to prohibit the widespread deployment of such surveillance tools with federal dollars,” Fulcher said in the press release. “It’s simple: if the federal government wants to access state and local systems’ data on citizens, they need to get a warrant.” The legislation would also put time limits on the retention of data federal authorities obtained, unless a court authorizes an extension or the data is needed as evidence for ongoing prosecution. The bill would also prohibit federal funds from being used to purchase or install surveillance devices, with some exceptions for systems used solely for toll collections on federally funded highways, school violence prevention programs, grants provided under the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act, and portable systems for specific law enforcement operations with a warrant. The bill, brought by Texas Republican U.S. Rep. Keith Self, was introduced July 15 and has not yet been voted on by a committee. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Idahoans have expressed concerns about surveillance cameras A number of Idaho cities statewide have contracts for automated license plate readers, called ALPRs, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. Flock is the most common and well-known brand of this type of camera. In July, nearly 100 residents filled the Caldwell City Council chambers, and about a dozen of them spoke about their concern about the city’s use of Flock cameras , the Idaho Press reported. All eyes on Flock as Idaho navigates surveillance technology across the state A 2025 Idaho state law prevents these readers from being used for anything other than “the investigation of felony, misdemeanor crimes, traffic accidents or to search for missing or endangered persons.” However, Twin Falls cameras were searched at least 631 times in March, May and June of 2026 for immigration-related searches, the Sun reported. The searches originated from outside Idaho, and later the Twin Falls Police Department changed its network sharing policies to avoid inadvertently running afoul of Idaho law and its own restrictions on immigration searches. In March, then-Jerome County Sheriff George Oppedyk used Flock cameras to search for his wife’s vehicle hundreds of times between July and September 2025, KMVT reported. Oppedyk retired in April. In early August, the Washington Post reported that at least 50 law enforcement officers across the nation had been charged with or accused of misusing the cameras to track women. Fulcher’s office regularly polls constituents who email him, and recent polls found that data privacy was one of their top concerns, Fulcher told the Idaho Capital Sun in an Aug. 12 interview. “The data privacy stuff, especially recently with the Flock cameras, that has got a lot of people on edge,” Fulcher said. items.body: A replica of the Liberty Bell sits outside of the Idaho Statehouse, as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) In May 1950, Idaho’s very own version of the Liberty Bell arrived in the Gem State. Idaho State Treasurer Julie Ellsworth (Photo courtesy of the Idaho State Treasurer’s Office) Nearly a year later, the bell found its home: Sitting prominently in front of grand steps leading up to the Idaho State Capitol — and being loudly rung by passersby. But before it was mounted at the state’s Capitol, the bell toured the state on the back of a pickup truck. And as Americans commemorate the nation’s 250th birthday this year, Idaho’s Liberty Bell is headed back on tour . “We want to have people experience the birth of a nation,” Idaho Treasurer Julie Ellsworth said in an interview. “… We want a memorable thing that touches every place of Idaho.” The tour starts Wednesday with a round of stops in East Idaho, starting in Pocatello and working its way further east, before visiting each of the state’s 44 counties. But how did Idaho even get its own version of the Liberty Bell? The bell — modeled after the cracked original in Philadelphia that has become a national symbol — was one of many cast and given to states in an effort to sell U.S. savings bonds, according to a history of the bell prepared by the Idaho State Historical Society. Idaho’s replica of the Liberty Bell, moved from its typical home, sits on the back of a Ford F-450 flatbed truck. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho State Treasurer’s Office) GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Trucking a state artifact This will be one of the few instances — outside of its recent restoration — when Idaho’s Liberty Bell has left its home at the Capitol. State officials designed this tour to mimic the original tour of the bell from 76 years ago. On its journey across Idaho, the state’s Liberty Bell will sit on the rear axle of a flatbed Ford F-450 pickup. The state is leasing the custom truck for free from Kendall Ford, an auto dealer in the Boise area, Ellsworth said. The new truck has a few more bells and whistles than the original truck had — like enhanced suspension and Spudjamin Franklin, one of many “Revolutionary Spuds” that the state treasurer created to celebrate America’s 250th anniversary. But it’s also missing something that the original truck, a custom Ford R-5 flatbed, had: a loudspeaker, which was used to promote the sale of U.S. savings bonds, according to Janet Gallimore, the executive director of the Idaho State Historical Society, which cares for the state’s artifacts and helped plan the bell’s recent restoration. The 1950 tour of Idaho’s replica of the Liberty Bell was to promote the sale of U.S. savings bonds. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho State Treasurer’s Office) “I … just love the symbology of the bell and what it means, what it meant for obviously the beginnings of our country and the founding of our country, but what that idea of liberty, justice, self-government means to people today. Because it’s a powerful symbol of those things that make us American,” she said in an interview. On the road, the bell will be encased in a cloth cover. At its stops in each county, it will remain on the bed of the truck for display. When will Idaho’s Liberty Bell be near you? Officials aren’t releasing a daily schedule of where the bell will be in each town at a given time until closer to the dates. But Ellsworth says every child that they see on this tour will get a copy of Spudjamin Franklin’s new graphic novel-styled autobiography, which she wrote. Ellsworth said she’ll try to join the tour as much as she can. “It is so symbolic of everything about liberty,” she said of the bell. “But it’s tangible. It’s touchable. It’s understandable.” On Wednesday, the bell will make its journey from Boise to Pocatello — before beginning a nearly three-week tour across East Idaho. items.body: A ballot drop box in Kitsap County, Washington, pictured Aug. 29, 2026. Washington is one of the eight states that conducts elections entirely by mail. (Photo by Jacob Fischler/States Newsroom) A Massachusetts federal judge on Monday declined the Trump administration’s request to overturn the temporary restraining order she signed last week that blocks the U.S. Postal Service from carrying out a rule placing new restrictions on mail-in voting. The 14-day order published Aug. 27 was not appealable, U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani wrote in a brief order Monday . But even if the order could be appealed, the administration would lose on the merits, Talwani wrote. “It is likely that the USPS lacked authority to issue the Final Rule and that the Final Rule is substantively unconstitutional and contrary to law,” she wrote. She dismissed the administration’s argument that the temporary restraining order came too close to Election Day as a “cynical interpretation” of the U.S. Supreme Court’s Aug. 24 decision that allowed President Donald Trump’s related executive order to move forward on procedural grounds. The high court found that Trump’s executive order, which directed the Postal Service to create the rule, could not be challenged until the rule itself was in place. It made no determination on the merits of the rule. “A Final Rule has now issued and, contrary to Defendants’ cynical interpretation, the Supreme Court has not endorsed the view that any challenge to the Final Rule is now too late,” Talwani, whom President Barack Obama appointed to the bench, wrote. She added that she disagreed with the USPS argument that the requirements of the rule, which would force states to overhaul their vote-by-mail systems ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections and to gain federal government approval of lists of voters who requested mail ballots, were “modest.” The administration is also fighting Democratic-led states and voting rights groups in the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals over Talwani’s temporary restraining order and in Talwani’s court over a longer pause of the final rule. Several Republican state attorneys general, representing Alabama, Florida, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota and Texas, joined the suit on the federal government’s side. The rule’s challengers say it is an inappropriate incursion of states’ power to administer elections, and would likely disenfranchise people who depend on mail ballots to vote. Trump has long claimed, without evidence, and despite his personal use of the service, that mail voting enables election fraud. The administration has said its rule is needed to ensure that noncitizens do not vote in federal elections, which studies have shown is rare. Trump issued the executive order March 31. States and voting rights groups immediately sued to stop it, but the legal battle heated up last week with the Supreme Court’s procedural decision on its emergency docket. The states and groups challenging the law quickly refiled their lawsuits to reflect that the rule had been published Aug. 21.

Idaho’s college savings program celebrated its 25th birthday last week with a new name, a new website and a milestone: $1.1 billion in assets for Idaho families to pay for education expenses. The new name, Idaho Education Savings Program , reflects the program’s versatility. Account holders can spend the money tax-free on more than college. Other educational expenses, including private school tuition or homeschooling materials, also qualify. The program was formerly known as the Idaho College Savings Program. items.body: Boise State University is denying wrongdoing in a public records dispute with a conservative lobbying group. Attorneys for Boise State say the university “acted in good faith” in responding to the Idaho Family Policy Center — even though the group received only two pages of university records, at a cost of $257.02. The IFPC filed a lawsuit on July 24 , stemming from a seven-month records dispute. The Christian lobbying group requested documents, data and correspondence related to a 2025 article authored by two Boise State researchers. The article said 35% of OB-GYNs left Idaho between 2022 and 2024, in the wake of the state’s near-total ban on abortion. The IFPC authored one of Idaho’s anti-abortion laws. The lawsuit alleges Boise State dragged out its response to the request for more than a month, withheld germane documents and charged for a costly legal review of the records that ultimately were released. “By refusing multiple requests for these documents, and rebuffing efforts to solve this matter without litigation, BSU has frivolously pursued its refusal,” the IFPC said in its lawsuit. In a response filed Tuesday, Boise State said it produced all documents that fell within the parameters of the request and did not delay its response. The university also defended the bill that it sent to the IFPC — which reflected 6.5 hours of staff review, including 3 hours of legal work. Idaho’s public records law is based in a presumption of openness. In other words, documents are considered public records unless they are specifically exempt from disclosure. The dispute between Boise State and the IFPC centers on two intertwined issues. The timing . The law requires public entities to release records to Idaho residents within three working days — although agencies can and frequently do claim an extension that pushes the timetable to 10 working days. In this case, IFPC policy analyst Grace Howat filed a records request on Dec. 10. Boise State responded on Dec. 23, within 10 working days. The university did not produce the records at this time, but instead sent an estimate — reflecting the potential cost of reviewing and producing the records. Boise State did not request payment at this time. On Jan. 8, Boise State sent a $257.02 invoice. IFPC paid the bill that day. Howat twice sent followup emails, asking about the status of the records request. “Am I able to receive the records I requested and paid for?” she wrote on Jan. 26. The university provided the two-page response on Jan. 27 — more than 10 working days after IFPC paid the invoice. But in Boise State’s response in court, attorneys defended the turnaround time. “(Boise State) denies (IFPC’s) characterization that (Boise State) ‘sat on the request for over a month.’” Carsten Peterson and Eric Stokes are representing Boise State in the case. They work for Hawley Troxell , a Boise-based firm prominent in education law . The invoice . Public agencies are required to cover some cost of retrieving records — their first two hours of staff time and the first 100 pages of paper records. Beyond that, agencies are allowed to bill their costs, but they aren’t required to do so. Boise State says the $257.02 invoice covers 6.5 hours of staff review, above the two “free” hours of employee time. IFPC is skeptical, noting that the two pages released by Boise State were unredacted. In their response, Boise State’s attorneys say that staff had to review documents beyond the two pages that were released. “(Boise State) denies the inference that 6 1/2 hours responding to Ms. Howat’s request was excessive.” What’s next? It’s unclear when the dispute may go to court. Both sides are seeking their costs and attorney’s fees. IFPC is also seeking the $257.02 in question, or a cost to be determined at trial. items.body: Crews are completing the new Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass south of Montpelier in Bear Lake County. (Photo by Julia Barton/Greater Yellowstone Coalition) Correction: This story was corrected to reflect that highway wildlife underpasses have also been built north of Bonners Ferry. Crews are nearing completion of a new wildlife underpass in southeast Idaho after the public, nonprofit agencies, conservation groups and government agencies pushed for years to protect migrating wildlife herds and drivers. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE The Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass is expected to be completed this fall along U.S. Highway 30, south of Montpelier in Bear Lake County, public officials and conservationists announced jointly this week. The wildlife crossing features three underpasses, as well as extensive fencing on either side of the project to direct animals like deer to the wildlife crossing. “We were seeing just all kinds of problems there; we were losing at least 100 deer a year,” Idaho Transportation Department public information officer Justin Smith said in an interview Wednesday. “Over 10 years, that is 1,000 animals we know we lost.” Officials also said those collisions cost drivers and taxpayers millions of dollars every year. “Our primary concern is the safety of the traveling public. Whether they are going through a construction zone or whether they are in a wildlife area, we want to keep people safe on our highways, and this is part of that effort,” Smith said. The Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass represents a partnership between the Idaho Transportation Department, Idaho Department of Fish and Game, the Greater Yellowstone Coalition, the Idaho Conservation League and Bear Lake County, officials said. This map depicts the project area for the Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass near Montpelier. (Map courtesy of Greater Yellowstone Coalition) “Rocky Point shows what’s possible when agencies, conservation and sporting groups and local communities work toward the same goal,” Matt Lucia, Idaho conservation manager at the Greater Yellowstone Coalition, said in a written statement. “(The Greater Yellowstone Coalition) has been part of this project for years — contributing time, energy and funds toward the effort. The next step is making sure the federal funding that made this project possible stays available.” To build the crossing, the Idaho Transportation Department secured a $20.8 million grant from the Federal Highway Administration’s Wildlife Crossing Pilot Program. Funding comes from the federal Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act that was passed by Congress and signed into law by former President Joe Biden in 2021. The federal grant was estimated to cover 98% of the construction costs, but the project may come in under budget, allowing the state to return some of the money to the Federal Highway Administration, Smith said. Idaho’s first major highway wildlife crossing was built outside of Boise in 2023 Need to get in touch? Have a news tip? CONTACT US The Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass near Montpelier is one of a handful of wildlife highway crossing in Idaho. In 2023, crews built the Cervidae Peak Wildlife Overpass on Idaho Highway 21 near Lucky Peak, between Boise and Idaho City. The Cervidae overpass features more than one mile of big game fencing to direct the animals to the safe crossing. Fish and Game officials installed a wildlife camera at the crossing to document how it is working. In 2024, state officials posted a time-lapse video showing more than 1,000 deer safely using the Cervidae Peak Wildlife Overpass between Oct. 17, 2024, and Dec. 18, 2024. In the early 2000s, crews also built wildlife underpasses north of Bonners Ferry on U.S. Highway 95 when they widened the highway, the Spokesman-Review reported. Smith said officials with the Idaho Transportation Department are studying other highway corridors with heavy wildlife populations, and the state is open to pursuing other new wildlife crossings as well.

(Getty Images) An advisory group has identified Idaho counties at high risk for opioid use disorder to target in its recommendations for the state’s use of opioid settlement funds. The Idaho Behavioral Health Council brings together the state’s three branches of government — legislative, judicial and executive — to provide recommendations to lawmakers about how to improve mental health and substance use issues statewide. The council on Friday finalized its recommendation that opioid settlement funds be prioritized for at-risk populations and communities. A summary highlighting some of the counties facing the highest risk of opioid use disorder included Kootenai, Benewah, Nez Perce, Bannock, Bear Lake, Clearwater, Boise and Ada counties. The state’s opioid settlement fund was created from a nationwide settlement with opioid manufacturers and may be used for certain, approved prevention or treatment projects. Last year, the Legislature approved spending $6.8 million of opioid settlement funds, according to a memo from the Division of Financial Management. Idaho Behavioral Health Council asks lawmakers to prioritize rural communities with opioid funding The council voted on its top priorities at a meeting in June, which included funding proposed for projects that focus on prevention for high-risk populations, behavioral health support for first responders, and developing the behavioral health workforce. Council members on Friday agreed to send a one-page summary outlining risk factors for opioid use disorder and highlighting which counties were most at-risk, using a 2024 report titled the Opioid-Related Overdose Vulnerability in Idaho: An Epidemiological Assessment. “This handout identifies risk factors for opioid use disorder and puts them in the context of Idaho, where those places are, where we may have more vulnerable folks, where we have had higher levels of overdose, where we have high levels of opioid prescriptions being written,” said Sara Omundson, administrative director of state courts and co-chair of the Behavioral Health Council. “All of this is based on research that was done over the last few years.” The council also agreed to ask the governor and state legislative budget writers to prioritize projects that serve rural communities in the state. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE What areas are at high risk for opioid use? Factors that may lead to certain populations to be at higher risk of misusing opioids include lower educational attainment, according to the risk factor summary the council included with its recommendations. Those without college experience are almost twice as likely to misuse opioids, the summary said. The summary also identified other Idaho counties at-risk because of factors such as high prescription rates and high narcotic arrests using data from the American Community Survey , the Idaho Prescription Drug Monitoring Program , and the Idaho State Police Statistical Analysis Center. The top counties at risk based on low average educational attainment are Shoshone, Lincoln, Minidoka, Owyhee, Adams, Benewah, Payette, Gooding, Jerome and Clark counties. The top counties for high opioid prescription rates are Nez Perce, Bannock, Bear Lake, Butte, Lewis, Shoshone, Benewah, Caribou, Gem and Lemhi. items.body: U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins (left) swears in Michael Boren as the under secretary for Natural Resources and Environment in her office on Jan. 20, 2026, at the USDA Headquarters in Washington, D.C. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE U.S. Sens. Ron Wyden, D-Oregon; Amy Klobuchar, D-Minnesota; and Martin Heinrich, D-New Mexico, requested a full investigation into Boren’s involvement and influence in the Cabin Creek Fire in a letter they sent to U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins. “Mr. Boren’s actions constitute potentially a misuse of taxpayer funds and put American families at further risk by diverting scarce resources from high-priority wildfires threatening communities elsewhere in the region and country,” the senators wrote. “We request a full investigation into the nature and extent of Boren’s involvement in response to the Cabin Creek Fire and a detailed accounting of the safeguards the agency has implemented or plans to implement to prevent political interference and conflicts of interest in wildfire response.” Need to get in touch? (Photo by Kelcie Moseley-Morris/Stateline) BOISE, Idaho — The group leading
items.body: Melanie Folwell, lead organizer for the ballot initiative in Idaho to restore abortion access, speaks to supporters at the Idaho Capitol in July. The nonprofit she leads, Idahoans United for Women and Families, is suing the state over a final segment of ballot language that will also appear in the statewide voter pamphlet. (Photo by Kelcie Moseley-Morris/Stateline) BOISE, Idaho — The group leading the effort to restore abortion access by ballot initiative in Idaho has filed a lawsuit against state officials over proposed language that will appear on the ballot and in a state-issued voter pamphlet. Idahoans United for Women and Families, the nonprofit organization that drafted the initiative — now called Proposition 1 — says the “yes” and “no” statements as prepared by Idaho officials violate the law guiding the initiative process and are confusing and misleading. Attorneys filed the lawsuit to the Idaho Supreme Court late Wednesday night. Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane stressed that the issue needs to be quickly resolved to meet upcoming ballot deadlines. The voter pamphlet must be printed by September 25, according to the law, and ballots need to be mailed to military and overseas voters about a week before that. McGrane said the state has paused production amid the litigation on the 850,000 copies of the voter pamphlet that need to be printed and mailed. “There was a good-faith effort to try and reflect each of the sides of the pro and con statements that were submitted to us,” McGrane told Stateline by phone on Thursday. “I think one of the biggest challenges that we’re going to see with Proposition 1 is that it’s a very complicated issue with a lot of nuance … and this isn’t a simple issue to consolidate down into a short, one-sentence statement.” Following the law, McGrane developed the language for the statements with Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador, who has been outspoken in his anti-abortion views for many years and recently appealed a federal judge’s decision that would protect abortion access in cases of threats to a pregnant patient’s physical and mental health. Labrador told Stateline in an emailed statement that his duty alongside the secretary was to clearly and concisely explain the effects of a “yes” or “no” vote and to fully inform Idaho voters, and said they applied the same legal standard to every measure that has been on the ballot. “Idaho voters deserve a straightforward explanation of what their vote will do,” Labrador said. Idaho Supreme Court orders officials to revise abortion ballot initiative language, impact statement There have been similar legal fights over abortion ballot language in other states. Activists on both sides of the issue in Missouri, for example, have spent years arguing over ballot language , both on the 2024 citizen-led amendment that restored legal access to abortion, and on the 2026 amendment referred by the legislature that would reinstate the ban. (Kevin Richert/Idaho EdNews) Heading to a meeting, flanked by House GOP Caucus Chair Jaron Crane, Moyle wasted no time getting to the point — Pemberton’s bill to rebrand Lewis-Clark State College as the state’s fourth full-fledged university. “He commented in passing that he hadn’t had time to ‘kill it yet,’” Pemberton, LC State’s president, said in subsequent emails to two other lawmakers. Pemberton stands by her account. When EdNews asked Moyle about the exchange this week, he chuckled. “She was persistent in the hallway all the time. I was just giving her a hard time.” Either way, the bill died, without a House hearing. Moyle, R-Star, insists he didn’t kill it, but says he doesn’t support the name change. Pemberton pledges to try again in 2027. “I better try one more time,” Pemberton said in an EdNews interview last week. “The campus community wants me to try again.” While renaming sounds cosmetic and simple, branding is essential. Supporters say university status better reflects a 133-year-old institution offering everything from associate’s degrees to master’s programs. A name is how an institution of higher learning markets itself to would-be students, prospective faculty members and possible business partners. A one-word change can change a lot. And the LC State renaming proposal was the most significant higher ed policy bill from the 2026 session. Emails between Pemberton and legislators — obtained by Idaho Education News through a public records request — offer an unusual and unfiltered behind-the-scenes look at how this bill died. The name change sailed through the Senate, but ran into high-placed resistance in the House, from Moyle and from his newly appointed House Education Committee chairman. Fundamentally, the bullet points haven’t changed. A rebrand aligns LC State with Idaho’s four-year universities — and distinguishes LC State from the public two-year schools that have “college” in their name. University status brings LC State in line with other teaching-oriented institutions in the West. It would help LC State compete with a new wave of competition: out-of-state online schools with “university” in their title. Pemberton sees it as simple marketing. A car dealership wouldn’t want its sign to list only one make of car when it has multiple options on the lot. (File photo courtesy of the Idaho State Department of Agriculture) Idaho state officials say they are continuing to push for full eradication of quagga mussels after again detecting the invasive species in the Snake River near Twin Falls earlier this month. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Although quagga mussels and larvae are small, state officials and conservationists say they cause giant problems because of how rapidly they reproduce. A mussel infestation can clog pipes used for irrigation and drinking water, which could have serious effects on the state’s economy, agriculture and recreation industries, officials said. “Our outlook is that not treating this infestation is not an option,” said Sydney Kennedy, a public information officer for the Idaho State Department of Agriculture said in an interview Wednesday. Gov. Brad Little agrees. Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little gives his State of the State Address from the House chambers on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “Other states have shown us what happens when invasive mussel infestations are allowed to establish before action is taken,” Little said in a written statement. “Those delayed responses have resulted in significant long-term management costs coming directly out of taxpayer pockets. Idaho has set the standard by responding aggressively. Our responsible strategy on the Snake River is proving to be effective, and we will continue making decisions that give us the best opportunity to eliminate quagga mussels to protect Idaho’s waters and the people who depend on them.” More than 1,700 different users, including municipal drinking water systems, depend on water from the Snake River, according to the state. Officials at the nonprofit Idaho Conservation League call the detection and presence of quagga mussels a no-win situation and one of the primary threats to the health of the Snake River. This month’s detection marks four consecutive years of finding quagga mussels in the Snake River near Twin Falls. In September 2023, state officials announced for the first time they had detected invasive quagga mussel larvae in water samples . Since 2023, the portion of the river where quagga mussels have been detected has shrunk, the Idaho State Department of Agriculture said. Fewer quagga mussels detected so far this year in Snake River State officials say the number of quagga mussels detected this year is down by 77% compared to last year. As of Aug. 14, the Idaho State Department of Agriculture has detected eight quagga mussel larvae, which are known as veligers, and seven adult quagga mussels. “We know what is at stake if invasive mussels gain a foothold in Idaho,” Idaho State Department of Agriculture Director Chanel Tewalt said in a written statement. “Our previous treatments have proven to be effective, and this level of containment is unprecedented among known quagga mussel infestations. items.body: U.S. District Judge B. Lynn Winmill ruled earlier this month that the state of Idaho cannot regulate abortion when a pregnancy threatens a person’s physical or mental health. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador appealed the decision, and the judge narrowed the ruling to only apply to the Boise doctor that challenged the law. (Otto Kitsinger for the Idaho Capital Sun) An Idaho federal judge has narrowed a previous ruling that had allowed abortions to protect a mother’s health or from self-harm to only apply to the Boise doctor who challenged the law. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador participates in a May 2026 roundtable at the Eisenhower Executive Office Building in Washington, D.C. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Attorney General’s Office) The narrowed ruling issued Tuesday means that Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador and the Ada County prosecutor may not enforce Idaho’s felony abortion ban in cases where Dr. Stacy Seyb administered the procedure because of serious risk of harm due to physical health or mental health concerns. Other doctors in Idaho will still be subject to Idaho’s near-total ban, which includes an exception to prevent the death of the mother but does not include exceptions to prevent her death from self-harm. Elective abortions are completely banned in Idaho. U.S. District Court of Idaho Judge B. Lynn Winmill narrowed the ruling at the request of Labrador, who argued in a recent motion that Winmill’s initial decision was too broad. Winmill agreed with Labrador, citing recent U.S. Supreme Court cases that ruled federal judges in most situations cannot issue “universal injunctions,” which block laws nationwide or more broadly than against the plaintiffs in the case. Winmill wrote “an injunction limited to Dr. Seyb will suffice to address the alleged harm.” Seyb was represented by attorneys from the Lawyering Project and Legal Voice in the case. “While we are disappointed in the ruling, it is only one step in the litigation,” Tanya Pellegrini, co-director of litigation at the Lawyering Project said in an emailed statement. “We will continue to stand with providers and their patients to ensure it is safe to be pregnant in Idaho.” Seyb is a maternal-fetal medicine physician who specializes in high-risk pregnancies. He challenged Idaho’s laws, testifying in court that he’s sent patients out of state amid health concerns because he did not feel comfortable providing abortions under the limited exceptions in Idaho’s law. Idaho’s criminal abortion ban allows an abortion to prevent the death of the mother, to treat ectopic or molar pregnancies, and in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester, if there’s been a police report filed. Doctors who provide abortions that don’t fall within those exceptions face two to five years in prison and revocation of their medical license. The judge denied Labrador’s request to fully eliminate the block on enforcement. Winmill remained “persuaded” abortions to protect women against serious health risks or against death from self-harm were constitutionally protected. Labrador on Aug. 20 also appealed Winmill’s decision to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, arguing the block defies the U.S. Supreme Court decision Dobbs v. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Around mid-day on a recent Tuesday in Twin Falls, a small plane landed on the tarmac at the Magic Valley Regional Airport but never taxied to the terminal. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Outside the fence surrounding the airport runway area, a group of five people watched through telescopes and binoculars as three white vans drove onto the tarmac. Around 20 men got out of the vans and boarded the plane as law enforcement oversaw the process, which took just over 30 minutes. One man was escorted back off the plane and into a van. According to a flight tracker, the plane then traveled to King County International Airport, or Boeing Field, which is located south of Seattle. Similar flights, operated by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, happen every Tuesday and Thursday at the Magic Valley airport. Shelly McDaniel and her husband Tim McDaniel record the entire boarding process for each ICE flight that operates out of the airport near Twin Falls. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Shelly McDaniel and her husband Tim McDaniel, who live about 30 minutes outside of Twin Falls, have watched every flight since they became involved in efforts to observe them on May 12. The McDaniels have recorded more than 500 detainees being flown out of the airport since flights began in early April. An ICE spokesperson told the Idaho Capital Sun the air operations provide “a network of air transportation to Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) 25 field offices to facilitate the movement of illegal aliens within the United States and their removal to destinations worldwide via air charter and commercial charter services.” “ICE is committed to the safety and welfare of those in custody throughout the entire transfer and removal process,” the spokesperson, who did not provide a name, said in an email. The spokesperson said in the Aug. 12 email that the agency had conducted 20 missions at the Magic Valley airport, also called Joslin Field. The agency’s Salt Lake City Field Office, which oversees Idaho, requests the flights “to support their operations which include the Magic Valley Region.” The Human Rights First ICE flight monitor has recorded 33 flights out of Twin Falls in 2026, and three flights out of the Boise airport. No other Idaho cities are listed. The federal immigration agency has a $1.8 billion contract with CSI Aviation, a private charter and cargo air transportation company, to operate the flights nationwide, according to federal spending data. Airport Manager Matt Barnes told the Sun in an email that the local airport does not have any formal agreement with ICE or CSI Aviation. “We are a public use airport that accepts federal grant funds, so we may not discriminate against aircraft operators who can safely operate at our facility,” Barnes said. ‘I think it’s wrong’; observers watch ICE flights because of due process concerns. items.body: Middleton School District trustees approved a name and tabled construction bids for the new elementary school at a special Tuesday afternoon meeting. The board tabled voting on a bid package for the new elementary school’s construction because potential bidders were not able to prepare bids in time. It will meet again next week to vote. The new Freedom Elementary, a name voted on by district constituents, won’t be far — in nomenclature or distance — from Independence Elementary, a new elementary school on the West Ada School District side of Star. Middleton’s new elementary will be located on the Canyon County side of Star, a city in two counties. It will serve one of the state’s fastest-growing areas and alleviate overcrowding in two elementary schools. In other action, trustees approved language for a $3 million supplemental levy, spread over two years, to fund teaching and classified positions, new curriculum, school resource officers, classroom technology and a “hot topic:” extracurricular transportation. The deadline for districts to submit ballot language is Friday, Aug. 28. After a failed supplemental levy in May, Middleton administrators made a round of cuts to staff, curricula and logistics. Constituents have been particularly frustrated by the lack of busing for extracurricular activities like sports, trustees said. Superintendent Marc Gee also presented language for a $2.8 million levy, an increase of about $2 per year per $100,000 of property value to taxpayers, over the $3 million option. Trustees didn’t like it. “I would say two dollars makes a big difference when it comes to taking care of our schools that we’re jamming full,” Dempsey said in favor of running the larger $3 million levy. Trustee Jay Clark suggested putting the transportation issue front-and-center in the levy. “That should give us some more votes, if that’s a hot topic,” Clark said. Trustees also approved a list of potential mascots for the new school: Elementary students will vote to choose between being Eagles, Falcons, Pioneers, Patriots or Stars. items.body: A new training center could enhance semiconductor education and apprenticeship programs through a partnership between Micron Technology Inc. and the College of Western Idaho. Micron Monday unveiled its 60,000-square-foot Micron Training Center near its Boise campus. The goal is to build semiconductor career pathways for community college students. “This unique, collaborative training facility accelerates new-hire readiness through an intensive onboarding boot camp and hands-on training in fab operations and manufacturing systems,” Micron said in a news release . The center houses up to 20 semiconductor process tools, designed to replicate Micron’s fab floor. CWI has received $3 million from Micron and the U.S. Department of Commerce, covering the cost of teacher pay, equipment and classroom space. “CWI and Micron have built a training environment where students learn on the same equipment they’ll operate in a world-class fab,” CWI President Gordon Jones said in the Micron news release. “This is what a decade of partnership looks like — a shared facility, tools, and commitment to building careers that matter for Idaho.” Beginning this fall, CWI will offer advanced mechatronics engineering technology and semiconductor manufacturing technology programs at the Micron center, in addition to course offerings at the college’s Nampa campus.

items.body: Firefighters on the Claremont Fire in Boise, Idaho on July 6, 2026. Drought across the Northwest has exacerbated wildfire conditions in the region. (Photo by Brenen Helgerson/ National Interagency Fire Center) The last weeks of summer find Oregon and much of the Northwest experiencing historic drought, exacerbating what has become one of the most active wildfire seasons in the state and region, according to state and federal climatologists and hydrologists. Beyond fish and ecological impacts, drought across Oregon, Idaho and Washington is causing water supply shortages for public water and electric utilities, costing farmers tens of millions of dollars in lost crops and leaving vegetation and soils dry and susceptible to fires. Wildfire and drought maps overlaid by Oregon’s State Climatologist Larry O’Neill on Monday during an online drought and climate outlook meeting hosted by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration show the summer’s wildfires popping up over historically dry areas of the state and region. About 4% of Oregon’s total land area — 2.4 million acres of mostly rangeland — has burned in the current fire season, most of which occurred within a one-month period. Overall, about 3.5 million acres have burned across the Northwest, including fires in and around Spokane that became some of the most destructive in Washington history. “Drought didn’t cause these ignitions, but they created the conditions with exceptionally dry vegetation and fuels that favor rapid fire growth and extreme impacts once those fires started,” O’Neill said. He and Catherine Fitzpatrick, a hydrologist at NOAA’s Northwest River Forecast Center, detailed water levels and conditions in the Northwest’s rivers, reservoirs and snowpack for a 90-day period, as well as the impacts of temperature anomalies. Even with a potential deluge of precipitation this winter in what O’Neill expects to be a “very strong” or “super” El Niño weather pattern, water reservoirs in the region are so depleted that there’s unlikely to be much carryover in water supplies into next year, the two warned. “Across the Pacific Northwest we’re substantially depleting our reservoir storage, and now we’re getting into kind of the later part of August and September, and reservoirs are being emptied out,” O’Neill said. “There’s little hope for carryover into the next water year, and then as I mentioned earlier, we’re seeing record low stream flows occurring in all three states.” Anomalous heat Most of eastern Oregon and southern Idaho have experienced summer temperatures 2 to 4 degrees Fahrenheit above normal, following what was the warmest fall and winter on record for the entire region, where temperatures in Oregon and Idaho were 3 to 5 degrees Fahrenheit above normal. Most of Oregon east of the Cascades has in the last 90 days experienced “extreme drought,” a NOAA designation indicating major crop and pasture losses, and widespread water shortages or restrictions. About 4% of Oregon in and around Grant, Baker and Wheeler counties in the eastern part of the state are in what NOAA classifies as “exceptional drought,” meaning it reached historic levels, among other indicators. It’s the second time since 2000 that Grant County has received the designation. Despite being surrounded by the Blue Mountains, the area saw the lowest snowpack on record this winter. About 8% of Idaho is experiencing exceptional drought, particularly in Owyhee, Twin Falls and Cassia counties in southern Idaho. Cuts to irrigation water supply for Idaho farmers have cost them $20 million so far according to crop insurance indemnities that are being paid out, O’Neill said, but the total cost is likely to be far higher as many claims won’t be processed until after the growing season ends. In the Yakima Basin in Washington, water users are receiving about 58% of their allotment. That includes the Roza Irrigation district, which supports more than $1.5 billion in annual agricultural revenue for the state.

As of August 2026, the commission authorized 67 schools, including four that have yet to open. Seven were virtual. There are 85 charter schools in the state, meaning the commission authorizes 79% of Idaho charters. The rest are authorized by school districts. What does the commission do? The commission authorizes and oversees most charter schools in the state. This includes authorizing schools to open and monitoring their financial, operational and academic success. How does the commission authorize a new school? The authorization process starts when a group hoping to found a new school contacts charter commission staff. Typically, that group includes the school’s founding board, which must establish a nonprofit corporation and establish 501(c)(3) status to apply. People interested in founding a charter school can take the Idaho Department of Education’s Charter 101 course. The founding group works with commission staff to submit an application packet that includes financial planning, school model information and evidence of student demand. The group then presents to the full commission, which can vote to authorize or deny the application. The commission has only denied a handful of applications over the last two decades, at least two received approval at a later date. Before opening, schools have a series of conditions to meet and have monthly meetings with commission staff to work toward completing pre-opening steps. The school’s governing board operates the school independently under its charter, subject to commission oversight. Schools are initially authorized for six years under a traditional charter. Schools authorized under the 2024 innovative charter law are authorized for three years. The commission meets every other month, typically in Boise. How does the commission hold existing schools accountable? The commission has standards that schools must meet related to finances, test scores and graduation rates, among other things. If a school meets those requirements, they continue operating with little commission interaction for their term. Schools that fail to meet a condition typically have a year to meet the metric. If they don’t, the commission can start proceedings to revoke the schools charter. However, a revocation has happened twice. Odyssey Charter School closed in 2015 and Nampa Classical Charter School closed in 2010, both shortly after opening. Another Choice, a virtual school, had its charter non-renewed in 2022 and was subsequently forced to close. Schools in good standing with the commission can have their charter renewed for 12 years if they meet certain criteria. Renewals can also be for a six year term. Who serves on the commission? The commission is made up of seven members appointed by the Governor. Commission staff handles the day-to-day work of supporting the commission and helping with charter oversight. Who makes up the commission staff? The commission faced significant staff turnover in recent years. Rachel Burk was hired in August 2025 as executive director. She filled a series of staff vacancies. The commission currently has two program managers, a finance program manager and an administrative assistant on staff. What is the charter commission’s annual budget? Taxpayers in Idaho are still waiting to get that number from a similar private school choice program that serves nearly nine and a half times fewer students, costs $950 million less and was enacted two months earlier. And it’s not for lack of trying. Between February and July, the Idaho State Tax Commission received seven public records requests related to the Parental Choice Tax Credit. A college faculty member, a hobbyist data analyst, a homeschool advocate, a former public school superintendent and two journalists filed requests seeking data that would shed light on who’s benefitting from the $50 million-a-year taxpayer-funded program. Four of those requests — including two from Idaho Education News — sought the number of tax-credit recipients who previously attended a public school. This data would test a selling point of the program: that it helps students who couldn’t otherwise afford a private education. That tally doesn’t include unofficial requests. Democratic lawmakers, who asked for data in March, weren’t included in a tracking sheet of records requests obtained by EdNews. Nearly all of the requests were denied. In an unsigned emergency docket opinion , the court’s conservative majority wrote the Trump administration is likely to prevail on its argument that 23 Democratic-led states do not have standing to stop his executive order to change how the U.S. Postal Service processes mail-in ballots. The majority justices also wrote that a lower court’s injunction is “causing irreparable harm,” but left open the possibility that the executive order could still be considered unconstitutional. “The Court’s disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell,” the majority wrote. The legality of a Massachusetts federal district court order, which paused the executive order to overhaul vote-by-mail systems before the Nov. 3 midterms, will now be decided by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit. Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented. In a lengthy dissent, Jackson wrote the ruling “needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections.” The principle of courts not altering voting systems too close to the election has been eroded, she said, amounting to a “Kafkaesque nightmare.” “States administering elections and the voting public that relies on them to do so deserve clarity, not caginess or confusion,” she wrote. It also asks USPS to collect voters’ names and addresses from state elections officials and directs the U.S. Justice Department to investigate and prosecute state officials who violate the order. The Postal Service issued a final rule Friday detailing how the process would be carried out. Whether an overhaul of mail-in ballots for each state could be completed in time for the Nov. 3 election remains to be seen, as vote-by-mail documents are sent to voters well in advance of Election Day.
